confirmed.regressionTest: Unit test: PdfRenderer.render({title:'CONTRAT', blocks:[{lines:['Łukasz Nowak']}]}) must NOT produce bytes containing '?ukasz' — either the glyph is preserved or the render throws/reports a lossy_transcoding failure.

confirmed.title: Document-generation and email audit events are written without user_id/agent_slug — orphaned rows invisible to every tenant-scoped read and to RLS
confirmed.currentBehavior: This write uses the canonical column vocabulary (`event_type`/`message`/`meta_json`) but still omits the tenant columns `user_id` and `agent_slug`, and it runs under the service role (RLS bypassed), so nothing rejects it. The same omission exists at src/app/api/pierre/email/send/route.ts:445 (`event: "email_sent_direct"`) and src/app/api/pierre/email/draft/route.ts:475 (`event: "email_draft_created"`), which additionally use the non-canonical `level`/`event`/`payload` columns. Every reader of this table requires the tenant key — src/app/api/pierre/use/audit-trail/route.ts:136 `.eq("user_id", userId).eq("agent_slug", "pierre")`, src/app/api/pierre/use/submit/route.ts:459-460, src/app/api/pierre/use/employee/[employeeId]/route.ts:331-332 — as does the RLS policy `using (auth.uid() = user_id)`.
confirmed.failureScenario: User A generates an HR document via /api/pierre/doc/generate. insertMissionLogIfNeeded lands a pierre_task_logs row with user_id = NULL. User A opens the audit trail or the employee 360 timeline: both filter `.eq("user_id", userId).eq("agent_slug","pierre")`, so the `document_generated_direct` event is never returned — the document exists but the record of who generated it, and under which mission, is not retrievable by the tenant. The row is likewise invisible under RLS to any authenticated client. If instead pierre_task_logs.user_id is NOT NULL, the insert errors and this route throws a 500 (`MISSION_LOG_CREATE_FAILED`) AFTER the document has already been generated and persisted — the caller sees a failure for an operation that in fact succeeded. Both branches are defects; the write simply has no tenant key.
confirmed.requiredCorrection: Add `user_id` (the authenticated user id already resolved in each route) and `agent_slug: "pierre"` to the insert payloads at doc/generate/route.ts:615, email/send/route.ts:445 and email/draft/route.ts:475, and normalise email/send + email/draft onto `event_type`/`meta_json` instead of `event`/`payload`. Make pierre_task_logs.user_id NOT NULL so a tenant-less audit write can never be persisted.
confirmed.regressionTest: Integration test: as user A, POST /api/pierre/doc/generate for a mission owned by A, then query pierre_task_logs with `.eq("user_id", A).eq("agent_slug","pierre").eq("event_type","document_generated_direct")` and assert exactly one row. Assert the same event is returned by GET /api/pierre/use/audit-trail?missionId=<id>. Repeat for /api/pierre/email/send and /api/pierre/email/draft.

confirmed.title: Un brouillon sensible (licenciement/sanction) préparé par Pierre s'affiche « Validé » en vert alors que son contenu n'a jamais été relu par un humain
confirmed.quotedCode:
if (requiresValidation && !TERMINAL_TASK.has(status)) artStatus = "awaiting_validation";
    else if (DONE_TASK.has(status)) artStatus = isComm && !isDoc ? "sent" : "validated";
confirmed.currentBehavior: Même dérivation : dès que la tâche documentaire est en succès terminal, l'artefact passe en `validated` ⇒ libellé « Validé », tonalité `success` (v1.ts:288, et status.ts:187 pour le présenteur canonique). Or le seul exécuteur documentaire qui renvoie `succeeded` est `prepareSensitiveDraft` (src/lib/pierre/v1/executors.ts:100-107), dont la sortie est explicitement `{ kind: "sensitive_draft", prepared: true, decision_taken: false }` — un dossier factuel préparé, JAMAIS validé. Le type `prepare_sensitive_draft` matche DOC_RE (via « draft ») ⇒ famille « Document » ⇒ statut « Validé ». La validation humaine du flux P8 porte sur la TÂCHE avant exécution (mission-service.ts:138-148 : approval_required ⇒ statut initial `awaiting_validation`), donc l'humain approuve la préparation AVANT que le brouillon n'existe : le contenu produit n'est relu par personne, et l'UI le présente ensuite comme « Validé ».
confirmed.failureScenario: Le dirigeant écrit « Préparer le licenciement de M. Durand ». SENSITIVE_RULES (analysis.ts:43) ⇒ action `termination`, tâche `prepare_sensitive_draft`, approval_required=true ⇒ tâche `awaiting_validation`. Le dirigeant approuve la validation (il approuve le fait que Pierre prépare). Le worker exécute prepareSensitiveDraft ⇒ `succeeded` avec `decision_taken: false`. Dans Documents du cockpit, la carte du dossier de licenciement affiche un chip VERT « Validé ». Le client comprend « le document est validé » alors que le dossier n'a été ni relu, ni approuvé sur son contenu — sur le sujet exact (licenciement) où le produit promet « aucune décision, préparation seulement ».
confirmed.requiredCorrection: Distinguer « préparé par Pierre » de « validé par un humain ». Un artefact issu d'une tâche en succès doit rester `draft`/« Préparé » (tonalité neutre) ; `validated` ne doit être atteint que par une décision humaine portant sur l'ARTEFACT (validation approuvée référençant l'artefact/version, cf. document-policy/contract-state), et `signed` que par une preuve de signature. confirmed.regressionTest: `deriveV1Artifacts([{ id: "t1", type: "prepare_sensitive_draft", status: "succeeded", approval_required: true }])` ⇒ attendre `status === "draft"` (ou « Préparé »), `statusView.tone !== "success"`, et surtout `statusView.label !== "Validé"`. confirmed.title: Runtime state-transition events record actor_type='user' with actor_id NULL — a human mission/task cancellation has no confirmer identity in the ledger
confirmed.currentBehavior: transitionMission (line 71) and transitionTask (line 57) are documented as "the only path to change status" and are the sole emitters of pierre_rt_events for transitions. Both append the event with actor_type only; they never pass actor_id, request_id or correlation_id, so EventRepo.append (repositories.ts:196) substitutes `e.actor_id ?? null`. cancelMission (line 286) calls `transitionTask(tx, ctx, t, "cancelled", "cancelled", "user")` and `transitionMission(tx, ctx.company_id, m, "cancelled", "cancelled", "user")` while holding the full TenantContext (ctx.user_id is available and unused; transitionTask's ctx is even narrowed to `{ company_id: string }`). Only two appends in the whole runtime carry an actor identity: mission-service.ts:122 (mission_received) and :239 (validation_<decision>). Every other user-attributed event — mission_cancelled, task_cancelled, task_ready after an approval — is stored as "a user did it" with no user.
confirmed.failureScenario: Admin A and admin B both have mission.cancel on company C. Admin B cancels a running termination mission, which cancels its queued tasks and their jobs. pierre_rt_events then contains type='mission_cancelled', actor_type='user', actor_id=NULL, request_id=NULL, correlation_id=NULL. Querying the timeline (EventRepo.timeline) to answer "who cancelled this mission and under which request?" is impossible — the ledger cannot distinguish A from B, or from an operator replaying a request. The same holds for every task_cancelled row.
confirmed.requiredCorrection: Widen the ctx parameter of transitionTask/transitionMission to the TenantContext (or an `{ company_id, user_id, request_id, correlation_id }` shape) and forward actor_id/request_id/correlation_id into EventRepo.append whenever actor === 'user'. Keep them null for 'system'/'worker'/'guard' actors.
confirmed.regressionTest: Integration test: create a mission as user U, call cancelMission with ctx.user_id=U, then assert that the pierre_rt_events row with type='mission_cancelled' has actor_id=U (and correlation_id non-null), and that the task_cancelled rows do too. Assert the invariant globally: no pierre_rt_events row may have actor_type='user' AND actor_id IS NULL.

refutedSummary.title: A hallucinated mission_id falls back to active[0] — an ambiguous « annule » cancels an unrelated mission
why:
The fallback is real and reachable — I confirmed ACTIVE_STATUSES genuinely intersects the canonical MissionStatus union (queued/planned/analyzing/blocked/awaiting_validation exist in state-machine.ts), so active[0] is not dead code. But the claimed harm rests on a premise the code contradicts: that the user confirms blind, "about a mission the user never asked to touch."

The confirmation is NOT blind. resolveCancellableMissionV1 returns {id, title} where title = the RESOLVED mission's real summary read back from V1 (`String(pick.summary ?? "mission")`), and proposal-builder.ts:87 stamps that into the label: `Annuler la mission « ${m.title} »`. The label is server-derived from the mission that will actually be cancelled — never from the model's hint string. CloneChatWorkspace.tsx:352 renders `{a.label}` as the card headline, followed by "Action irréversible — votre confirmation est requise." So in the auditor's own scenario the user asks about Paul and is shown, verbatim, "Annuler la mission « <Marie's onboarding summary> » — Action irréversible". The consent is specific to the resolved target, and summary is populated at INSERT (mission-service.ts:119, `summary: analysis.summary` on createMission), so it is not an empty placeholder in practice.

Stacked protections around it, all verified:
1. Never fabricates a target: hallucinated id + no active mission ⇒ pick is null ⇒ `if (!m) return null` (proposal-builder.ts:85) ⇒ no proposal, no button at all. A model-invented id can never conjure a cancellable mission.
2. Tenant-scoped: the V1 list is fetched with the server-pinned `x-pierre-company` header, which V1 re-verifies against membership. Only the caller's own company's missions are ever candidates — no cross-tenant reach.
3. RBAC + product-access: apiCancelMission → cancelMission does `requirePermission(ctx, "mission.cancel")` (mission-service.ts:287) behind `withProductAccess(req, "write_standard")`.
4. The client never holds or supplies the target: useCloneChat.ts:398 posts `{ proposalId }` only; execute/route.ts:101 reads missionId from the PERSISTED proposal payload (`String(p.missionId ?? "")`). The client-side applyTool fallback in governed-turn.ts:116 is filtered out before render (useCloneChat.ts:332), so it is never executable.
5. Proposal expiry (P16D, fail-closed) + SHA-256 command ledger gate the execute.

Residual (real but not the claimed defect): on a hint that matches nothing while other missions ARE active, returning active[0] instead of null is a sharp edge — the last line of defense is the human reading the label. Tightening `resolveCancellableMissionV1` to return null when a non-empty hintId fails to match would be a cheap hardening. But the high-severity outcome as stated — an irreversible cancellation of an unrelated mission slipped past an uninformed confirm click — is not what the code does: the confirmation names the actual mission being cancelled.

The active[0] fallback is real code, but the claimed impact ("cancels an unrelated mission ... after a confirm click about a mission the user never asked to touch", severity high, unsafe/irreversible autonomous decision) is overstated and does not follow. Three verified facts break the consequence chain:

(1) NO AUTONOMOUS EXECUTION. buildAndPersistProposal only PERSISTS a proposal; it triggers no effect. Grepping every non-test caller of `runGovernedCommand` / `/api/assistant/execute` across src: the only caller of the execute route is useCloneChat.executeAction (useCloneChat.ts:394), whose only caller is `onAction` (CloneChatWorkspace.tsx:99), which is the `onClick` handler of the Confirmer button (CloneChatWorkspace.tsx:355). There is no auto-confirm, no autonomy mode that skips the click, no server-side self-execution. The cancel cannot happen without an explicit human click.

(2) THE CONFIRM CARD NAMES THE MISSION THAT WILL ACTUALLY BE CANCELLED — not the hallucinated one. proposal-builder.ts:84-87 derives BOTH the payload and the label from the SAME resolved object `m`, so the displayed title and the cancel target can never diverge. And `m.title` = `String(pick.summary ?? "mission")` where `pick` is exactly the mission cancelMissionV1 will cancel. `summary` is a real, populated column: api.ts:29/34 selects it in the list item, and mission-service.ts:119 sets `summary: analysis.summary` at creation. So the label renders as e.g. «Annuler la mission "Onboarding de Marie"» — the true target, by name.

(3) THE USER SEES IT BEFORE ACTING. useCloneChat.ts:332 explicitly FILTERS OUT the stale client-derived action_preview (the second, independent fallback at governed-turn.ts:116), so ONLY the server-resolved proposal label is rendered — there is no path that shows title A while cancelling mission B. CloneChatWorkspace.tsx:352-353 renders that label as the card headline plus "Action irréversible — votre confirmation est requise." above the Confirmer button.

So in the stated scenario ("Fais le nécessaire pour Paul, laisse tomber le reste"), the user is shown a card that truthfully names the unrelated mission and flags it irreversible, and must click Confirmer. The system never acts on the hallucinated id; it acts on a real, server-resolved, named mission only after an informed human confirmation. That confirmation card IS the disambiguation surface. There is no duplicate external effect, no false success (cancelMissionV1's 2xx follows V1 actually performing the cancel), and no tenant leak (the V1 mission list is company-scoped via the tenant context / RLS).

Residual (real but lower severity): silently substituting active[0] for an unresolvable hint is poor design — returning null and asking "which mission?" would be better, and the same loose fallback is duplicated at governed-turn.ts:116. Also byHint searches `items` rather than `active`, so a hint can select a terminal mission (which then fails closed on the invalid state transition). These are ambiguity/UX defects, not the claimed high-severity irreversible unsafe-autonomous-action.

refutedSummary.title: The « who » ambiguity gate is satisfied by ANY capitalized word, and the live path never resolves the name to a real employee
why: The exact claimed input is intercepted by a guard the auditor did not read, ~60 lines below the quoted snippet, inside the very function under audit. `isVagueDirective("Fais le nécessaire pour Paul.")` returns true (NFD-folded match on /\ble necessaire\b/), which (a) pushes a HIGH-priority `"what"` clarification into missing_info, and (b) replaces the catch-all rule set with `request_missing_info` / `clarification_required` — so the `create_task` catch-all at analysis.ts:159 is the *else* branch and is never reached, meaning the executors.ts `{ outcome: "succeeded", kind: "task_created" }` chain never starts. `approval_required` therefore computes to TRUE (analysis.ts:177) and next_best_action is "Collecter les informations manquantes", not "Exécuter les tâches faibles risques". mission-service.ts closes the door a second, independent time regardless of action kind: line 146 forces task status `awaiting_info` (never `ready`, therefore never queued, therefore the worker never runs it) and line 193 forces missionStatus `awaiting_info` — the mission cannot reach `queued`, let alone `done`. The live path is covered: mission-service.ts:97 calls cognitiveAnalyze, and cognitive-analyzer.ts:153 runs `raiseFloor(analyzeInstruction(...))` as the authoritative floor, with applySafetyFloor (lines 136-137) UNION-ing base.missing_info and OR-ing base.approval_required, so the LLM planner cannot erase the "what" question. The second claimed example ("Envoie le nécessaire avant Vendredi") contains "le nécessaire" and is blocked identically. This is a documented, tested fix: src/lib/pierre/__tests__/p16d-ambiguous-instruction.test.ts describes verbatim the state the auditor reports (missing_info: [], approval_required: false, proposed_tasks: [create_task], "c'est donc le nom propre — et lui seul — qui faisait taire la clarification") as the ALREADY-CORRECTED prior behavior, and asserts the current behavior over 7 vague directives plus an inverse-regression suite. Residual grain of truth (not the claimed defect): hasSubject is indeed satisfied by any capitalized token and no employee resolution occurs on createMission — but on its own that yields no fabricated action and no false 'done'.

The claim is written against a stale version of src/lib/pierre/v1/analysis.ts (its quoted line 63 is now a comment; the regex it quotes lives at 85-90). The claimed reproduction is gated upstream by the P16D vague-directive check that sits in the SAME function, and its regexes were built for exactly this sentence.

Concrete trace for the claimed input "Fais le nécessaire pour Paul.":
1. isVagueDirective() folds accents + lowercases, then matches /\ble necessaire\b/ -> true.
2. When vague, analyzeInstruction pushes {id:"what", priority:"high"} into missing_info AND replaces the rule set with request_missing_info / intent "clarification_required". The catch-all create_task branch the claim depends on is the ELSE of that ternary and is never taken. So the executors.ts create_task path returning {outcome:"succeeded", output:{kind:"task_created"}} is unreachable for this input.
3. The hasSubject leniency ("Paul" silencing the "who" question) is therefore moot: the "what" gate fires instead.
4. Live path: mission-service.ts:97 calls cognitiveAnalyze, whose deterministic floor is analyzeInstruction. Any high-priority missing_info forces mission-service.ts:146 to set the task status to "awaiting_info" (never "ready", so the enqueue loop at :182 skips it, queued stays 0), and :193 sets missionStatus = "awaiting_info" BEFORE the queued>0 branch. The mission cannot reach 'done' and nothing executes.
5. With the LLM planner enabled, applySafetyFloor merges missing_info: [...base.missing_info, ...(llm.missing_info ?? [])], so the "what" high-priority floor survives whatever the model proposes and still forces awaiting_info.
6. Every mission entry point (CloneChat included) funnels through src/lib/pierre/v1/api.ts:26 -> createMission, so nothing bypasses the gate.

Empirical proof: `npx vitest run src/lib/pierre/__tests__/p16d-ambiguous-instruction.test.ts` -> 16/16 pass. That suite asserts on the exact claimed sentence: missing_info contains "what"/high, approval_required === true, the only proposed task is request_missing_info, intent === "clarification_required", next_best_action does NOT match /Exécuter/i. Its header documents this very defect as already reproduced and corrected. The claim's second example ("Envoie le nécessaire avant Vendredi") also contains "le nécessaire" and takes the same clarification path.

Residual, NOT the claimed defect: hasSubject is still literally lenient — a capitalized weekday/city silences the "who" question for a NON-vague instruction (e.g. "Prépare le dossier avant Vendredi." -> create_task with empty missing_info). But that produces only an internal task + internal summary (external_side_effect:false), employee_id stays null and no employee is ever asserted as resolved, so it does not yield the claimed outcome (a vague directive fabricating a 'done' mission with invented HR work). The file also documents why a bare "no operational rule matched" must not be treated as ambiguity: it would block legitimate requests like "Prépare l'onboarding de Sarah lundi".

refutedSummary.title: `cancel_mission` (risk=irreversible) also substitutes an arbitrary target: an unresolvable mission_id silently becomes "the first active mission"
why: REFUTED — the "silent substitution" is not silent, and it cannot execute an undisclosed target. Three protections the auditor did not follow: (1) DISPLAY==EFFECT INVARIANT. In proposal-builder.ts:84-87 the confirm label and the executed payload are derived from the SAME resolved object in adjacent lines: `payload = { missionId: m.id }` and `label = "Annuler la mission « " + m.title + " »"`. So when active[0] is substituted, the card names THAT mission. useCloneChat.ts:325-328 pushes the server label with `risk: "irreversible"`; CloneChatWorkspace.tsx:383-388 renders it verbatim above "Action irréversible — votre confirmation est requise." plus a separate "Confirmer" button. The client holds no payload (only proposalId); /api/assistant/execute re-loads the persisted proposal scoped to {companyId,userId} and cancels exactly the id whose title was shown. The claim's own failure scenario concedes the true title is displayed and then relies on the user not reading it — that is a UX-disambiguation hardening (refuse when ambiguous / require exact id match), not a defect where the system acts on a target it never disclosed. (2) The `byHint` over `items` instead of `active` is bounded by the state machine: cancelMission -> transitionMission -> assertMissionTransition(mission.status,"cancelled") (mission-service.ts:75) rejects a terminal mission, V1 returns 4xx, isTerminalStatus -> `failed`, zero effect. (3) Scope/RBAC: perms.canCancelMission (action-policy.ts:35-36) + requirePermission(ctx,"mission.cancel") in V1, and the list is company-pinned via x-pierre-company re-verified against membership, so active[0] is always one of the caller's OWN missions, never a foreign one. Finally, "on n'invente jamais de cible" is honored in its real sense: the resolver only ever returns a REAL existing tenant-scoped mission id (never a fabricated one) and returns null — no button at all — when none exists; the identical "model ref, else first non-terminal" fallback is the deliberate pattern already in openai/governed-turn.ts:116.

The substitution is real, but the claimed impact is overstated. (1) Not silent: the resolved fallback mission's title is rendered verbatim to the user in the confirmation card. proposal-builder.ts derives BOTH the executed payload (missionId = m.id) and the label ("Annuler la mission « <m.title> »") from the SAME resolved mission object, so displayed target and executed target cannot diverge. useCloneChat.ts:325-328 injects that server label into an action_preview, and CloneChatWorkspace.tsx:383-387 renders it as the card headline followed by "Action irréversible — votre confirmation est requise", with the "Confirmer" button underneath. The user is shown the real target's name before any effect. (2) Not autonomous: cancel_mission is RISK "irreversible" ⇒ requiresConfirmation; the only execution path is an explicit user-triggered POST /api/assistant/execute carrying the proposalId. No auto-execute path exists. (3) The stale-hint sub-claim (byHint searched over items, not active) fails closed at the engine: a hint on a done/cancelled mission yields a proposal, but cancelMissionV1 → /api/pierre/v1/missions/[id]/cancel → apiCancelMission hits state-machine.ts where TERMINAL_MISSION_STATUSES = ["done","cancelled","archived"] and cancelled: ["archived"] ⇒ invalid transition ⇒ 4xx ⇒ isTerminalStatus ⇒ {ok:false, terminal:true}, no effect. So: no duplicate external effect, no false success, no tenant leak (list is scoped by x-pierre-company, re-verified against membership), no unconfirmed irreversible decision. What survives is a genuine product-precision inconsistency worth fixing (the "on n'invente jamais de cible" comment is contradicted by active[0]; byHint should be scoped to active; an unresolvable explicit hint should return null), but its consequence is UX misdirection that still requires the human to confirm a card that truthfully names the other mission — not the claimed unsafe irreversible autonomous effect.

refutedSummary.title: A restrictive clause in a conflicting instruction is never parsed, never binds the plan, and is never recorded: only the permissive half drives execution
why: All three load-bearing assertions are factually wrong against the real code. (1) "The regex guard never sees the restriction": on the deterministic path the per-task objective IS the raw user instruction (analysis.ts:119 `objective: `${r.intent} — ${text.slice(0, 140)}``), so evaluateGuard({text: at.objective}) at mission-service.ts:135 receives the user's own words including the restrictive clause. (2) "Never recorded": MissionRepo.insert persists `instruction: input.instruction` verbatim and EventRepo.append writes `mission_received` in the same transaction (mission-service.ts:113-122), so the clause is durably in the mission row and the CloneTrace log. (3) The claimed harmful consequence — "task queued → executed, enqueuing the external-contact outbox row the user explicitly forbade" — is unreachable. analyzeInstruction can only emit task types from OPERATIONAL_RULES/SENSITIVE_RULES action kinds (reminder, deadline_reminder, request_missing_info, classification, operational_summary, low_risk_notification, create_task, prepare_sensitive_draft); it can never emit `email_send`. The `reminder` executor has `external_side_effect: false`, contacts nobody, and enqueues NO outbox row — so decideValidation is not even called with external_side_effect:true (it returns AUTO_EXECUTE, and what auto-executes is an internal reminder note). Only awaitingExecutor(...) instances write to the outbox, and the sole one with external_side_effect:true is `email_send`, which the analyzer cannot produce. Defense in depth: the LLM planner is off unless AI runtime is "production" (isCognitivePlannerEnabled), the email_send executor returns "awaiting_integration" (never "succeeded"), and communication-event-registry pins outbox kind "email" to allowedChannels ["in_app"] with payload-supplied policy IGNORED and unknown kinds quarantined. There is no autonomous external-contact path out of the v1 mission runtime in any autonomy mode, so "ne contacte personne sans mon accord" is honored structurally. What remains is a feature gap (no first-class user-constraint parser in the v1 mission planner; the /agents/pierre/use/submit surface does parse "ne pas envoyer"/"n'envoie pas"), not a correctness or safety defect: no forbidden action executes, no external row is written, and the instruction is recorded.

The bad outcome is not reachable from the specified input; the claim's own trace is wrong at three load-bearing points.

(1) It asserts `external_side_effect:true` for the co-planned reminder task. Both sources are FALSE: analysis.ts sets `external_side_effect: false` on every OPERATIONAL_RULES task, and `executorExternalSideEffect("reminder")` returns false because the `reminder` Executor is declared `external_side_effect: false`. So the `||` at mission-service.ts:136 evaluates to false.

(2) It asserts `decideValidation` returns EXECUTE_AND_NOTIFY. With `external_side_effect:false`, mode 'normal' + `AUTO_EXECUTE_ACTIONS.has("reminder")` + risk 'low' returns AUTO_EXECUTE. (Immaterial to approvalRequired, but shows the trace was not executed.)

(3) The stated harm — "enqueuing the external-contact outbox row the user explicitly forbade" — never occurs. The `reminder` executor's entire body is a `return` statement: it touches no DB, no outbox, no channel, no recipient. The ONLY executors that call `OutboxRepo.enqueue` are the `awaitingExecutor(...)` instances registered for task types `email_send` / `document_generate` / `file_store` / `notification`. The deterministic analyzer can never emit those types: `type: r.action` is drawn exclusively from {reminder, deadline_reminder, request_missing_info, classification, operational_summary, low_risk_notification} + create_task fallback + prepare_sensitive_draft. `low_risk_notification` resolves to `internalNotification` (registered first, preserved by `if (!REGISTRY[e.type])`), which writes an IN-APP row (`kind:'internal'`, `delivered:"in_app"`), not an external contact. So on the reproduced path the mission executes, contacts nobody, and creates zero outbox rows — the user's "ne contacte personne" is not violated by any executed effect.

(4) The claim's premise that the guard "never sees the restriction" because `at.objective` is model-authored is also false on the deterministic path: `objective: `${r.intent} — ${text.slice(0, 140)}`` embeds the user's RAW instruction (the 88-char scenario text fits entirely), so `evaluateGuard({text: at.objective})` does receive "ne contacte personne sans mon accord". It simply has no PROHIBITED_PATTERNS entry for a user-authored constraint — its patterns target sensitive HR acts (termination/sanction/protected characteristics/harassment/medical).

Even the most favorable salvage construction fails: to reach an outbox-writing executor you need task type `email_send`, which requires the LLM planner (isCognitivePlannerEnabled → real AI production mode) to emit it. Even then `toActionKind("email_send", …)` → `create_task` → auto-executes → outbox row `kind:"email"` — but communication-event-registry binds kind "email" to `allowedChannels: ["in_app"], requiredChannels: ["in_app"], recipientStrategy:"task_target"`, so no external party can ever be contacted from this path. The delivered artifact is an in-tenant in-app notification.

What remains true is descriptive: no module parses user prohibitions, and EventRepo.append records only `{guard, decision}`. That is a genuine MISSING FEATURE (no constraint-extraction/binding layer for user-stated restrictions), and worth a product backlog item — but it is not the claimed defect: no forbidden contact is executed, no external-effect outbox row is created, and no gate is bypassed. Under the reproducer rule ("if you cannot construct a reachable path to the bad outcome, it is refuted"), this is refuted.

refutedSummary.title: normalizeDecision defaults to "approve" — a model-intended REFUSAL of a termination/sanction validation is silently turned into an APPROVAL
why: The claimed critical failure — a model-intended refusal being SILENTLY turned into an executed approval of a human-only termination — is refuted by two protections the auditor did not look at. (1) The label shown to the human is derived from the SAME normalized value that goes into the executed payload (proposal-builder.ts:92-94): if normalizeDecision falls through to "approve", the proposal card literally reads "Approuver cette validation". There is no divergence between what is displayed and what executes. (2) The claim's load-bearing premise — "the user clicks the single 'Confirmer' button" — is factually wrong: CloneChatWorkspace.tsx:379-392 renders the action label as a headline, plus an explicit "Action sensible — votre confirmation est requise." warning, immediately above the Confirmer button. The model has no execution path at all: decide_validation is effect:true/requiresConfirmation:true in action-policy.ts, the server only persists a proposal, and /api/assistant/execute runs only when the user POSTs the proposalId from that click (useCloneChat.ts:371-384), after an actor+company-scoped load and a fail-closed freshness check. So no validation is ever approved without an explicit human click on a card whose visible text states "Approuver cette validation" — the human-only decision gate holds, and the durable actor_type:"user" audit entry records the truth (the human did approve what the card said). What genuinely remains is a lower-severity correctness/UX wart, not the claimed critical bypass: normalizeDecision is an approve-by-default free-text parser (same at governed-turn.ts:108), and the tool JSON schema does not enum-constrain `decision` (structured-output.ts: arguments = {type:"object", additionalProperties:true}), so a user who asked to REFUSE can be presented with an "Approuver" card. It should be an allowlist with null => no proposal. But it does not flip a human refusal into an approval on its own, and it does not defeat the human-only floor.

The trigger is real but the claimed impact is overstated, so the critical severity is refuted. Real part: chat/route.ts:508 calls buildAndPersistProposal with the raw structured.tool_call and NO validateToolArgs gate (unlike governed-turn.ts:216, which does gate but is not the live chat path), and structured-output.ts types tool arguments as z.record(z.string(), z.unknown()) / additionalProperties:true with no enum on `decision`. So decision:"refuser" and an omitted decision both reach normalizeDecision and both return "approve".

Where the claim breaks: it asserts the refusal is "silently turned into an approval" and that "the one human gate protecting the MUST_NOT list has been flipped from refusal to approval by the model". It is not silent and the gate is not flipped. In proposal-builder.ts the persisted payload and the displayed label are computed from the SAME `decision` constant on adjacent lines (92-94), so they can never diverge: a payload of {decision:"approve"} ALWAYS carries the label "Approuver cette validation". CloneChatWorkspace.tsx:383-387 renders that label as the card headline immediately above the button, together with "Action sensible — votre confirmation est requise." The human therefore sees the word "Approuver" verbatim and must click Confirmer. /api/assistant/execute only executes a proposal the human confirmed (proposalId, SHA-256 claim), and decideValidationAction further requires the "validation.decide" permission and stamps the real human actor. There is no autonomous model decision and no false audit trail: the durable validation_approved event records that the human approved — which is exactly what the human was shown and clicked.

The downstream mechanics the claim cites are accurate (escalated -> ready -> queued with no guard re-check in decideValidationAction), but that chain only fires behind a human clicking a button on a card that literally says "Approve this validation", so it is not an unsafe autonomous decision. The genuine residual defect is fail-open input normalization of lower severity: a model-intended refusal is offered to the user as an APPROVE card, so the user cannot reject via CloneChat when the model says "refuser", and a user who reads only the assistant's prose and clicks Confirmer without reading the card headline would approve what they meant to refuse. Correct fix is fail-closed (unrecognized/absent decision => return null, no proposal) plus applying validateToolArgs on the chat path. That is a UI-fidelity/validation bug, not a critical breach of the human-only gate.

refutedSummary.title: Worker executes the executor BEFORE the CloneGuard black hard-block, committing durable side effects on a guard-blocked task
why:
The ordering observation is literally correct (executor.run() at worker.ts:76 precedes the guard check at :79, and awaitingExecutor enqueues an outbox row at executors.ts:115), and the re-queue path is real (state-machine.ts:64 allows escalated->ready; mission-service.ts:159 creates a validation for escalated tasks). But the claimed HARM -- "the dismissal email is already sitting pending in the outbox for the communications dispatcher" -- is impossible, blocked by two independent fail-closed layers the auditor did not look at.

(1) The outbox kind "email" is IN_APP-ONLY by server policy. communication-event-registry.ts:64 declares "email" with allowedChannels: ["in_app"], requiredChannels: ["in_app"]. communications.ts:120 only creates an email delivery `if (policy.allowedChannels.includes("email"))` -- false. An email-channel delivery row can NEVER be created from this kind. The auditor assumed kind:"email" means "an email"; the registry says otherwise, and the registry is the sole authority ("A policy supplied in an outbox payload is IGNORED").

(2) The row fail-closes at recipient resolution before ANY delivery row exists. The executor payload is `{ objective: task.objective }` -- it carries NO `task_id` key (task_id is a separate column). objectRefForEvent (communications.ts:39) therefore yields objectId = payload.task_id ?? null = NULL. resolveCommunicationRecipient -> loadObjectAndTarget (communication-recipient-resolver.ts:37-38) returns exists:false for a mission_task with no objectId, so resolved:false / recipient:null. communications.ts:107 then audits "communication.suppressed", calls markOutboxProcessed, increments res.blocked and CONTINUES -- no recipient row, no delivery row, no in-app message, no email.

(3) dispatchCommunicationDeliveries claims ONLY from pierre_rt_communication_deliveries (communications.ts:218, pierre_rt_claim_communication_deliveries) -- never from the outbox. Every caller (runtime-scheduler.ts:178, runtime-action-handlers.ts:146, the dispatch route, e2e-control-plane.ts:125) runs createCommunicationIntents first, so nothing bypasses the fail-close.

(4) OutboxRepo.pending (repositories.ts:236) -- the un-joined `status='pending'` query the report cites as the leak -- HAS NO CALLER anywhere in src (grep of OutboxRepo\. hits only executors.ts:115). The real drain is communications.ts:66, i.e. the fail-closed path above.

Residue is inert: a suppressed outbox row marked processed, plus (for low_risk_notification) a pierre_rt_notifications row inserted with NO recipient_user_id, which listInternalMessages (communications.ts:431) filters out via `recipient_user_id=$2` -- invisible to every user. And the external-effect executors never call a provider by construction (they return awaiting_integration, never succeeded). Net: no human-only HR decision is executed, no external effect, nothing reaches a human. The worker comment is imprecise about ordering; the "high severity dismissal email pending in the outbox" scenario cannot occur.

The ORDERING is real (worker.ts:75-79 runs `executor.run()` before it inspects `exec.guard`, so a guard-black task can leave a durable `pierre_rt_outbox` row behind), but the CLAIMED IMPACT — "the dismissal email is already sitting pending in the outbox for the communications dispatcher" — is false at three independent, verified layers. There is no external effect, no false success, no unsafe autonomous HR decision.

(1) NO EXTERNAL EMAIL IS POSSIBLE FOR THIS OUTBOX KIND. `awaitingExecutor("email_send", "email", true)` writes an outbox row with `kind: "email"`. The server-authoritative policy for the `"email"` kind in communication-event-registry.ts declares `allowedChannels: ["in_app"], requiredChannels: ["in_app"]`. communications.ts:118-121 builds deliveries strictly from `policy.allowedChannels`, so the email branch is never taken. The P8.4 dispatcher can NEVER create an `email` delivery for a task outbox row — the only channel it can ever produce is an in-app message to an employer operator. The "dismissal email sent to Marc" outcome does not exist in the code.

(2) THE ROW PRODUCES ZERO DELIVERIES ANYWAY. The executor's payload is `{ objective: task.objective }` — it contains no `task_id`. `objectRefForEvent` (communications.ts:39) resolves the `"email"` kind to `{ objectType: "mission_task", objectId: payload.task_id }` = **null**. `resolveCommunicationRecipient` → `loadObjectAndTarget` (recipient-resolver.ts:37-38) returns `exists:false` for a null mission_task objectId ⇒ blocker `object_not_found_in_tenant` ⇒ `resolved:false`. communications.ts:107 then short-circuits: the intent is persisted with `status:"blocked"`, audited as `communication.suppressed`, and the outbox row is marked processed. No recipient row, no delivery row, nothing to dispatch. The dispatcher `dispatchCommunicationDeliveries` claims from `pierre_rt_communication_deliveries` — a table that has no row for this event. It fails closed.

(3) EVEN IF A RECIPIENT RESOLVED, IT IS AN INTERNAL ESCALATION, NOT THE ACTION. The `"email"` policy's `recipientStrategy` is `task_target` with `fallbackStrategy: "tenant_owner"`, and the resolver sets `resolved_email` from `pierre_rt_companies.signatory_email` (the employer), never an employee address. The frozen content is the generic `task.notification` template rendered from only `{object_label, action_path}`. So the worst reachable outcome is an in-app notice to the employer pointing at the cockpit — the opposite of an autonomous dismissal.

Also note the claim's cited mechanism is wrong: nothing calls `OutboxRepo.pending` (repositories.ts:236) — grep shows zero callers outside its own definition. The real pipeline is the company-scoped query at communications.ts:66, which is gated by the classification/recipient logic above.

Finally, the task itself does NOT get a false success: the worker escalates it (`blocked_by_guard`), records attempt `"blocked"`, and returns `"blocked"`. And the hard-blocked ACTION kinds (`termination`, `dismissal`, `sanction`, …) have no executor in REGISTRY at all, so `resolveExecutor` returns the fallback that writes nothing — the only way to reach a black guard on a *writing* executor is black-by-`risk==="critical"`, whose entire footprint is a never-deliverable outbox row or an orphan `pierre_rt_notifications` row with no `recipient_user_id` (invisible to `listInternalMessages`, which filters `recipient_user_id=ctx.user_id`).

VERDICT: real ordering/hygiene wart worth fixing (guard should be evaluated before `executor.run`, and the code comment overstates what it does), but severity is LOW — stray unreferenced rows — not HIGH. It fails closed; no duplicate/unsafe external effect follows.

refutedSummary.title: The ActionKind is never persisted — the execution-time CloneGuard re-derives it from task.type (an executor key), losing the HARD_BLOCK / APPROVAL_ONLY structural floor
why:
REFUTED — the ActionKind verdict IS persisted, just not as a raw string, and the human-only floor lives in the queue-admission rule, not in the execution-time guard.

1) The ActionKind guard/decision at createMission is persisted as THREE durable artifacts, all derived from the real `at.action`:
   - `status` = "escalated" when guard.level === "black" (every HARD_BLOCK ActionKind), or "awaiting_validation" when approvalRequired (every APPROVAL_ONLY ActionKind, and everything decideValidation gates) — mission-service.ts:138-148;
   - `approval_required` — a REAL persisted boolean column (repositories.ts TaskRow:31, insert columns line 117, bound param line 121);
   - a ValidationRepo row + validation_requested event (mission-service.ts:159-169).

2) There are exactly THREE production call sites that put a job in the queue (grep for `enqueueJob(` outside tests returns only these):
   - mission-service.ts:184 — guarded by `if (t && t.status === "ready")`. A HARD_BLOCK ActionKind can never be "ready": black ⇒ status "escalated"; APPROVAL_ONLY / decideValidation ⇒ "awaiting_validation". Neither is "ready", so neither is ever enqueued.
   - mission-service.ts:267 — inside decideValidationAction, only on `mapped === "approved"`, by a user holding `validation.decide`. That IS the human decision.
   - worker.ts:101 — dependent unlock, explicitly gated by `unmet === 0 && !dep.approval_required`, i.e. it reads the persisted column that the real ActionKind produced.
   worker.ts:75-76 is the ONLY executor invoker in the codebase.

3) Therefore the failure scenario is unreachable as stated. A termination/sanction task (action="termination" ⇒ HARD_BLOCK ⇒ black; or riskForAction ⇒ "critical") never reaches `guardFor` at all — it is escalated at creation, never queued. It can only reach the worker AFTER an explicit human approval, which is precisely the human-only floor being asserted. And even then the executor registered for type "prepare_sensitive_draft" is the draft preparer that returns `{ prepared: true, decision_taken: false }` with `external_side_effect: false` — it never takes the sensitive action.

4) The "model-controlled ActionKind" sub-claim is also wrong: the model controls `type` (free text), but `action` is derived SERVER-SIDE by `toActionKind(type, title)` (cognitive-analyzer.ts:26-42), with `riskForAction`/`sensForAction` forcing termination/dismissal/sensitive_medical to critical+restricted, and raiseFloor/applySafetyFloor only ever RAISING risk/sensitivity (maxRisk/maxSens). A free-text type the model invents resolves to the fallback executor (executors.ts:138-144), which returns "unsupported" with no side effect.

Residual (not the claimed defect): `guardFor`'s `task.type as ActionKind` cast is genuinely sloppy — the execution-time guard is a weaker, redundant defense-in-depth net (only risk/sensitivity/text carry). Hardening it (persisting `action`, or mapping type→ActionKind) would be a cleanup, but it does NOT remove any floor: no HARD_BLOCK/APPROVAL_ONLY action can be executed autonomously, because it can never enter the queue without a human approving it.

The MECHANISM is real (AnalyzedTask.action is not persisted; guardFor casts task.type as ActionKind, and for a sanction the persisted type is "prepare_sensitive_draft", so HARD_BLOCK.has() is false and risk "high" !== "critical"), but the BAD OUTCOME — a human-only HR decision executed without a human — is unreachable. Three gates upstream of guardFor:

(1) The human-only floor is enforced where the ActionKind actually exists: createMission (mission-service.ts:135) calls evaluateGuard with the REAL at.action ("sanction"/"termination"/...), which IS in HARD_BLOCK, so line 144 sets status="escalated". Only status==="ready" tasks are enqueued (line 182). A HARD_BLOCK task is therefore NEVER queued at creation. decideValidation independently returns HUMAN_APPROVAL_REQUIRED for all 11 approval actions.

(2) The only production path from escalated/awaiting_validation into the queue is decideValidationAction (mission-service.ts:267) — an explicit human approve requiring the "validation.decide" permission. The worker's automatic dependent-unlock (worker.ts:101) is guarded by `!dep.approval_required`, and mission-service.ts:138 sets approvalRequired = ... || !guard.allow, which is true for every guard-black task, so the worker can never auto-enqueue one. mission-service.ts:150 is the ONLY production TaskRepo.insert (all other hits are tests).

(3) Even once a human has approved and the task reaches guardFor, no executor in REGISTRY can take a sensitive decision. Every sensitive analysis emits type="prepare_sensitive_draft", whose executor returns decision_taken:false with external_side_effect:false. email_send/document_generate/file_store return "awaiting_integration", NEVER "succeeded". There is no executor keyed "termination"/"sanction"/"dismissal"; such a type hits the fallback and returns "unsupported". Additionally the critical-risk HARD_BLOCK actions (termination, dismissal, sensitive_medical) STILL trip black at the worker via `input.risk === "critical"`, because risk IS persisted.

The residual delta is only that a human-APPROVED escalation runs its prepare-draft executor and lands "succeeded" instead of being re-escalated by a second black check — a degraded defense-in-depth re-check, not a bypass of the human-only floor. It is also plausibly the intended semantic: state-machine.ts:64 makes escalated→ready a LEGAL transition and decideValidationAction deliberately unlocks escalated tasks; if guardFor saw the true ActionKind, every human-approved sanction would loop back to escalated forever and prepareSensitiveDraft would become unreachable dead code.

refutedSummary.title: CloneGuard's termination text pattern is dead for every real French conjugation — trailing \b makes /\b(licenci|renvoy|...)\b/ unmatchable
why: The auditor quoted stale/nonexistent code. src/lib/pierre/v1/cloneguard.ts:42 is not a pattern line at all — it is part of a comment block. The real PROHIBITED_PATTERNS entry is at line 59 and has NO trailing \b on the termination stems: /licenci|renvoy|renvoi|\bvir(e|es|er|ez|ent)\b/. A phase named P16D already found and fixed exactly this defect; its comment (lines 41-53) describes the old \blicenci\b hole verbatim as the reason for the change, and it also added normalizeGuardText() (NFD accent-fold + lowercase) so accented forms fold before matching. The closing \b is retained ONLY on vir(e|es|er|ez|ent) to avoid over-matching "virement" (payroll bank transfer). I executed the actual regex against the actual normalizer: "Licencier Marc pour faute grave" -> true, and likewise licencié / licenciement / licencie / renvoyer / renvoi / vire-le -> true, while "virement bancaire" -> false. The claim's precise failure scenario (evaluateGuard({action:"create_task", risk:"low", sensitivity:"normal", text:"Licencier Marc pour faute grave"})) is the `benign()` helper in src/lib/pierre/__tests__/p16d-human-only-lexical-net.test.ts, which asserts prohibited_actions CONTAINS "termination_decision". So textHits is non-empty, the line-88 red branch fires (allow:false, requires_approval:true), and the label IS recorded. No unmatchable pattern, no missing escalation.

The finding quotes a line that does not exist in the file. The claimed regex `/\b(licenci|renvoy|vir[ée]r?)\b/i` (trailing \b after the alternation group) has already been fixed; line 42 is a comment, and the pattern table now starts at line 58. The current termination pattern is `/licenci|renvoy|renvoi|\bvir(e|es|er|ez|ent)\b/` — no trailing boundary after the alternation. The only remaining `\b` is scoped to the `vir(...)` branch alone, deliberately, so that `virer` fires while `virement` (a payroll bank transfer) does not.

Crucially, the fix is self-documenting: lines 41-53 are a P16D comment that describes the exact bug the finding claims, in the past tense, and explains the remedy ("JS \b is ASCII-only: a trailing \b after a truncated stem (\blicenci\b) can only match when the next character is NON-word, so it matched 'licencié' (the é creates the boundary) while missing every real inflection — 'licencier', 'licenciement', 'licencie'"). The same pass added normalizeGuardText() (NFD + combining-mark strip + lowercase) and closed two sibling holes (`\bsyndic\b` missing "syndicat", `\bhandicap\b` missing un-accented "handicape").

I replayed the exact failure scenario. normalizeGuardText("Licencier Marc pour faute grave") => "licencier marc pour faute grave"; /licenci/ matches => textHits = ["termination_decision"] => the `textHits.length > 0` branch at line 88 fires => the function returns level "red", allow:false, requires_approval:true, prohibited_actions:["termination_decision"]. It does NOT return green/allow:true as the finding asserts. Verified matching across licencier / licenciement / licencié / licencie / renvoyer / renvoyé / "virer Marc", with "virement de salaire" correctly NOT matching. The text backstop fires; the escalation path is reachable, not dead.

The finding's reasoning about JS \b semantics is sound in the abstract — the quoted regex does return false on the scenario when tested standalone — but it is aimed at code that is no longer present. This is a stale finding against an already-remediated file.

CAVEAT (does not change the verdict): I hit a concurrent-rewrite condition — Read and sed returned different bytes for line 59 within the same session. The file oscillates between the P16D version above and an earlier revision `/(licenci|renvoy|vir[ée]r?)/i` with `const normalized = input.text ?? ""` (no accent folding). BOTH revisions lack the trailing \b and BOTH match "Licencier Marc pour faute grave", so the defect is refuted under either. Worth pinning down separately, since the older revision loses accent-folding coverage.

refutedSummary.title: An ambiguous provider timeout is recorded as a definitive `failed`; ChannelEnvelopeStatus has no unknown/reconciliation state and the B37 send carries no idempotency key, so any resend duplicates the email
why:
REFUTED — unreachable / dead code, and the quoted catch is not even reachable from the real provider.

1) No such function. The claim names `sendChannelEnvelope`; the only export at that site is `sendChannelMessage` (runtime.ts:36).

2) Zero product callers, zero persistence, zero retry. Grepping the whole repo for `sendChannelMessage`, `channels/runtime`, and relative `../runtime` imports yields exactly ONE importer: `src/lib/cloneos/channels/__tests__/channels-b33.test.ts:518`. No API route, cron, worker, or lib imports it. `sendChannelMessage` returns an in-memory `ChannelSendResult`; nothing writes `envelope.status` to any store, and there is no "resend a failed envelope" function or retry loop anywhere. The failure scenario's required steps — "the envelope is persisted as failed", "an operator (or any future retry loop) resends" — have no code to execute them. The claim itself concedes "no product caller — tests only".

3) The quoted catch (runtime.ts:148) cannot fire from the real Resend adapter. `resendChannelProvider.send` wraps its entire live call in its own try/catch (providers/resend.ts:210-251) and returns `{ok:false, error: mapResendError(err)}` instead of throwing. A socket/abort timeout therefore lands on the `if (!providerResult.ok)` branch (runtime.ts:164), not the exception branch quoted at :148. Only an injected throwing adapter (i.e. a test) reaches line 148.

4) The live send is gated several times over anyway: `getActiveChannelProvider` returns `mockChannelProvider` unless CHANNEL_RUNTIME_MODE=production AND CHANNEL_DEFAULT_PROVIDER=resend AND RESEND_API_KEY AND EMAIL_PROVIDER=resend; and `resendChannelProvider.send` short-circuits to a `dry_run_...` id unless EMAIL_DRY_RUN=false AND EMAIL_SEND_LIVE=true (resend.ts:187).

The one true residual observation is a hardening gap, not this defect: the actually reachable live-email path is `src/lib/pierre/email/pierre-email-actions.ts:89` → `sendEmailProduction` (email-production/runtime.ts) → `createResendEmailProviderAdapter` → `resendChannelProvider.send`, and that path also passes no Idempotency-Key. But it likewise has no retry-of-failed and no resend surface, so no duplicate-email outcome can be constructed there either. No reachable path to the bad outcome ⇒ refuted.

The code-shape observations are accurate, but the claimed IMPACT (a duplicate real email reaching an employee) does not follow — every load-bearing link in the harm chain is absent, and the behavior fails in the SAFE direction.

1) The quoted function is not `sendChannelEnvelope` — it is `sendChannelMessage`, and it has ZERO product callers. A repo-wide grep for `sendChannelEnvelope|sendChannelMessage` returns only the definition (runtime.ts:36), docs (B33_CONTACT_CHANNEL_IDENTITY_LAYER.md), and tests (channels-b33.test.ts). The quoted catch block at runtime.ts:148 is unreachable from product code.

2) The REAL product email path never touches runtime.ts. It is src/lib/pierre/email/pierre-email-actions.ts:89 -> sendEmailProduction (email-production/runtime.ts) -> provider-adapter.ts -> providers/resend.ts. The B33/B37 orchestrator containing the quoted catch is bypassed entirely, so the "failed" status it produces is never written anywhere in production.

3) There is NO envelope persistence. `buildChannelEnvelope` / `ChannelEnvelope` appear only inside the channels module, its tests, and docs — no repository, no DB table, no queue, no API route. A "failed" envelope is an in-memory object returned to the caller and garbage-collected. There is nothing for an operator to look at, and nothing to resend.

4) There is NO resend/retry mechanism. A case-insensitive grep for `retry|resend(Envelope|Failed)|reschedule|re-send|renvoy` across src/lib/cloneos/channels/** returns NO MATCHES. The live B39 orchestrator explicitly documents `// Call provider exactly once` and returns without retrying. The failure scenario's pivotal step ("an operator or any future retry loop resends the failed envelope") has no mechanism to occur. The finding's own parenthetical ("no product caller — tests only — so this is latent") already concedes this and contradicts its own "the employee receives the HR email twice" claim.

5) The behavior FAILS CLOSED. An ambiguous post-ack timeout is recorded as `failed` — i.e. it UNDER-claims success. The dangerous direction (a false `sent`/`delivered` for a message that never went out) never occurs. Conservatively recording a maybe-sent as failed is safe on its own; the only harm would come from an automated retry, which does not exist.

6) Reaching the live send at providers/resend.ts:227 additionally requires stacking CHANNEL_RUNTIME_MODE=production + CHANNEL_DEFAULT_PROVIDER=resend + RESEND_API_KEY + EMAIL_PROVIDER=resend + EMAIL_SEND_LIVE=true + EMAIL_DRY_RUN=false — all defaulting safe (mode=mock, send_live=false, dry_run=true), with router.ts falling back to mock on any gap.

The accurate residue (catch collapses timeout to `failed`; ChannelEnvelopeStatus lacks an unknown/reconciliation state; providers/resend.ts:227 sends no Idempotency-Key) is a HARDENING PREREQUISITE that must be satisfied BEFORE anyone builds envelope persistence or a retry loop. It is not a present duplicate external effect, false success, tenant leak, or unsafe autonomous decision. Severity "medium" is overstated for current behavior.

refutedSummary.title: In production mode a misconfigured Resend silently falls back to the MOCK provider, which returns ok:true and marks the envelope `sent`
why:
REFUTED — the real production email path is fail-closed elsewhere, and the path the claim targets is dormant and non-persisting.

1) The ONLY product caller of an outbound email send is `src/lib/pierre/email/pierre-email-actions.ts:89` → `sendEmailProduction` (`src/lib/cloneos/channels/email-production/runtime.ts`). That runtime is the hardened B39.1 orchestrator and it does exactly what the auditor says is missing: in `live` mode it calls `getDefaultEmailProviderAdapter(config)`, which returns `null` when `resend_api_key_present` is false (provider-adapter.ts:122-125), and runtime.ts:298-317 then returns `ok:false, sent:false, status:"blocked_provider_not_configured"` with a `send_blocked` audit event. There is a second belt: `createResendEmailProviderAdapter().send()` re-checks `resendChannelProvider.isConfigured()` and returns `ok:false` ("RESEND_API_KEY manquant"). A misconfigured Resend in production therefore BLOCKS, it never fabricates a delivery. Note also that `getDefaultEmailProviderAdapter` never returns a mock in live mode — the mock adapter is only ever hand-injected by tests.

2) The function the claim actually indicts, `sendChannelMessage` in `src/lib/cloneos/channels/runtime.ts` (the claim calls it `sendChannelEnvelope`, which does not exist), is the legacy B33/B37 surface. Grep for `sendChannelMessage|getActiveChannelProvider|getProviderForMode` over all of `src/` returns only `channels/runtime.ts` itself, the router, and test files (`channels-b33.test.ts`, `channels-b37-resend.test.ts`, `pierre-b37-production-smoke.test.ts`). No route, no worker, no executor, no cron uses it.

3) The failure scenario's core assertion — "every outbound channel envelope is persisted as status:'sent' with a mock_ provider_message_id" — is false: nothing in `src/lib/cloneos/channels/**` persists anything. `envelopes.ts` header: "Pure, no async, no DB." `events.ts` header: "Callers persist events; this module only builds them." A grep for `sql\`|supabase|INSERT INTO|db` across the whole channels layer (excluding tests) returns zero hits. `sendChannelMessage` returns an in-memory object to a caller that does not exist.

4) Even the "silent" part is wrong: the mock result is self-labelled (`provider_message_id = mock_<envelopeId>_<ts>`, `meta = { mock: true, simulated_at }`), and runtime.ts:180 passes both the id and the meta into `buildSendSuccessEvent`, so any hypothetical consumer sees `mock:true`.

5) Finally, `status:"sent"` in this legacy layer was never a claim of real delivery even on the happy path: a FULLY configured Resend still returns `ok:true` with `dry_run_<id>` whenever `EMAIL_DRY_RUN=true` or `EMAIL_SEND_LIVE=false` (resend.ts:187-207 — and those are the defaults, per .env.local `EMAIL_DRY_RUN=true`, `EMAIL_SEND_LIVE=false`). So "mock fallback marks it sent" is consistent with the layer's own semantics, not a divergence from them.

The mock-in-production fallback in router.ts:34 is a stylistic wart in dead code, not a production defect: it cannot be reached by any product code, it persists nothing, and the live email path it would supposedly corrupt is a different, fail-closed runtime.

UNREACHABLE / DEAD CODE, and the real path is already fail-closed.

But execute/route.ts:73-79 enforces a fail-closed freshness gate BEFORE any command/effect, and proposal-expiry.ts:18 defines PROPOSAL_TTL_MS = 15 minutes (P16D expiration, whose header comment names the exact "role/company/headcount/entitlement changed in the meantime" risk this claim raises). refutedSummary.title: contract-readiness `document_hash_ok` is a tautology — the document_hash_drift blocker (and the approval-invalidation audit it triggers) can never fire
why: The auditor's syntactic observation is correct — `document_hash_ok` is always true as wired from contracts.ts:180 (both operands derive from the same `$6` bind at contracts.ts:269, so content_hash === canonical_hash always), making `block("document_hash_drift")` unreachable. But the claimed IMPACT is refuted: content drift is not undetected, and `signature_ready` does NOT stay true. The real "content that was approved" record is not on the version row at all — it is the append-only `pierre_rt_contract_approvals.content_hash`, written at approval time from the then-current `v.canonical_hash` (contracts.ts:328) and re-verified on EVERY readiness evaluation by the count query at contracts.ts:159-161, which filters approvals on `content_hash is not distinct from $4` where `$4 = version.canonical_hash` (the CURRENT value). If any path mutated canonical_hash after approval, that count drops to 0, so contract-readiness.ts:122 fires `block("insufficient_approvals")` at BOTH finalization and signature stages, and line 141 computes `signature_ready = ... && input.approvals_valid >= input.required_approvals` = FALSE. finalizeContract (contracts.ts:342) and prepareContractSignature (contracts.ts:418, `if (!readiness.signature_ready || !readiness.ready) throw`) both hard-refuse. Every contract policy sets required_approvals: 1 (contract-policies.ts:50/85/88), so there is no 0-approval escape. Three more layers: (1) the DB trigger `pierre_rt_contract_version_guard` raises 'a finalized/signed contract version is immutable (content frozen)' on any change to content_hash/canonical_hash once final/signed (v14 sql:135, v15 sql:50; proven by p83-b2g-contract-immutability.itest.ts:35); (2) no in-system path can rewrite canonical_hash while approved — generateContract requires STATUS_OK.generate = ["draft","changes_requested"] and createContractVersion requires MUTABLE = ["draft","changes_requested"] (contracts.ts:115-120); (3) contracts.ts:269 is the ONLY writer of those two columns repo-wide. The sole residual consequence is cosmetic: content drift is audited as `contract.generation_blocked / insufficient_approvals` instead of emitting `contract.approval_invalidated` (the branch at contracts.ts:344 is only reachable via the template-fingerprint half). That is a dead-flag / event-label nit on a fail-closed path, not the medium-severity document-integrity hole claimed.

The syntactic observation is correct — through `resolveReadiness`, `document_hash_ok` is a self-comparison and `block("document_hash_drift")` cannot fire from the service (the only test that hits it, p83-b2g-contract-readiness.itest.ts:61, injects `document_content_hash: "DRIFTED"` straight into the pure function, a state the service can never produce). But the claimed FAILURE — "approval bound to the exact content is inert / signature_ready stays true under content drift / drift defence is single-layer and silent" — is refuted: no reachable state produces a bad outcome, and the content-binding control is NOT the version row, it is an append-only ledger.

1) The hashes cannot diverge. The ONLY writer of these columns is contracts.ts:269, which sets `content_hash=$6, canonical_hash=$6` from one bind param. The other version writers (contracts.ts:97/123, employees.ts:62/69) insert both as NULL. And once the version is final/signed, `trg_contract_version_guard` (v14 migration, lines 131-143) raises `a finalized/signed contract version is immutable` on any change to content_hash/canonical_hash/template_fingerprint. So no "regeneration, backfill, admin fix-up, amendment/activation path" mutates canonical_hash independently — I grepped every write to `pierre_rt_employee_contract_versions`; signatures.ts only moves workflow_status.

2) The record of "the content that was approved" DOES exist — the claim looks for it in the wrong table. `pierre_rt_contract_approvals.content_hash` is written by approveContract (contracts.ts:326-328) from `v.canonical_hash`, and the table is insert-only (triggers `trg_contract_appr_no_upd` / `trg_contract_appr_no_del`, v14:74-77). Readiness consumes it at contracts.ts:159-161, doing the SAME hash equality against the immutable ledger row rather than against itself.

3) That ledger check is load-bearing and fail-closed, so the defence is not inert. Every contract policy has `required_approvals >= 1` (contract-policies.ts:50 default, :85, :88 — none is 0). If canonical_hash ever changed after approval, the count query returns 0 → `insufficient_approvals` (contract-readiness.ts:122) → `ready=false` AND `signature_ready=false` (line 141 requires `approvals_valid >= required_approvals`). So the claim's "signature_ready stays true" is impossible.

4) A stale approval can't even survive to a gate. STATUS_OK.generate = ["draft","changes_requested"], so you cannot regenerate while `approved`. The state machine (contract-state.ts:17-20) forces approved → changes_requested → draft, and the only exit from changes_requested is createContractVersion, which mints a NEW version row (hashes/approved_fingerprint NULL) and resets the contract to draft. Returning to `approved` (STATUS_OK.finalize=["approved"]) therefore always re-runs approveContract, which writes a fresh ledger row bound to the current canonical_hash and rewrites approved_fingerprint. I could not construct any input/state where a contract reaches finalize or prepare_signature with an approval bound to different content.

Residue (not the claimed defect): the expression at contracts.ts:180 is genuinely redundant/dead, and if drift were ever forced in, the refusal would be audited as `insufficient_approvals` instead of emitting `contract.approval_invalidated` (contracts.ts:344) — an audit-label nuance on a refusal that still happens, not a document-integrity failure. The claim's own scenario is explicitly conditional on hypothetical future code ("If any future/parallel path mutates..."), which is a code-smell/defence-in-depth note, not a medium-severity defect.

refutedSummary.title: enforceDocumentGuard is wired to exactly one action (download) — the fail-closed finalize / submit_signature / delete / modify rules are dead code, and approveVersion records no content hash at all
why:
The grep fact is true (enforceDocumentGuard is only called from downloadDocument at documents.ts:244), but every security consequence the auditor derives from it is refuted by protections they did not look for.

1) THE FAILURE SCENARIO HAS NO CALLER — AND CANNOT HAVE ONE. `documents.ts` has exactly three production importers: `contracts.ts:21` (create/version/submit/approve/finalize), `signatures.ts:20` (createVersion only), `runtime-compensation-execution.ts:16` (archiveDocument only). Grepping `src/app/**` for `createDocument|createVersion|approveVersion|finalizeVersion|downloadDocument` returns **No matches found** — no API route touches the document layer. The single production `createDocument` call is `contracts.ts:263` with `document_type: policy.document_type`, and contract policies map ONLY to `employment_contract` / `contract_amendment` (contract-policies.ts:44-45). There is no code path in the product that can create a `disciplinary_document` or `payroll_variable_document` at all, so the claimed blast radius is empty.

2) THE hr_director APPROVAL IS ENFORCED — just not by the guard. `disciplinary_document` carries `approve_roles: ["OWNER","ADMIN","HR_DIRECTOR"]` (document-types.ts:68). `approveVersion` calls `assertDocumentTypePolicy({action:"approve"})`, whose `approve` branch blocks `role_cannot_approve_document_type` (document-policy.ts:56-59), and `finalizeVersion` HARD-requires `v.status !== "approved" → throw` (documents.ts:161). So even in the hypothetical direct-call scenario, a disciplinary document cannot reach `final` without an OWNER/ADMIN/HR_DIRECTOR approval. The claim "bypassing the hr_director approval" is false on the merits.

3) "NO CONTENT-TO-APPROVAL BINDING WHATSOEVER" IS FALSE TWICE. (a) Structurally: content is immutable per version — there is no in-place modify-version operation anywhere (`assertMutable`, and signatures.ts:416 creates a NEW version for the signed artifact rather than mutating), and `createVersion` explicitly resets the approval (`status='draft', approved_by=null, approved_at=null`, documents.ts:113). Approval binds to a version row whose content_hash/file-ids ARE the content; any change forces a new unapproved draft. That is exactly the `approval_invalidated_by_change` / `modify_version` invariant, enforced by the data model — which is why an `approved_content_hash` column would be redundant. (b) Explicitly on the only real path: `pierre_rt_contract_approvals(template_fingerprint, content_hash)` (contracts.ts:326-328), `approved_fingerprint` (329), readiness `document_hash_ok` → `block("document_hash_drift")` (contract-readiness.ts:118,124), `finalizeContract` even emits `contract.approval_invalidated` on drift (contracts.ts:344-348), and `pierre_rt_signature_requests.approved_content_hash` is persisted (contracts.ts:433) with a reuse-with-different-content conflict (contracts.ts:411). The submit_signature "approval + matching hashes" invariant is genuinely enforced.

4) THE DELETE RULES ARE NOT DEAD. `softDeleteDocument` enforces inline exactly the guard's two delete_document rules: `legal_hold` (documents.ts:205) and `signed` (documents.ts:206).

5) THE FINALIZE FILE/HASH RULES ARE NOT DEAD. `finalizeVersion` re-runs `assertFileAttachable` on every artifact (the P16D retro-quarantine fix, documents.ts:171-173) and refuses without a content hash (174, 181) — the guard's file_not_clean / scan_not_clean / content_hash_missing rules.

6) template_not_published / missing_required_fields at finalize are enforced for the reachable flow at the GENERATION stage by the readiness engine (contract-readiness.ts:84, 111), by explicit design documented at contract-readiness.ts:77-79: once a version is generated its content is frozen in the canonical hash + clean artifact, so later stages verify artifact/approvals/drift rather than raw input fields.

What survives is only that the guard's docstring ("the single choke-point a real service calls") overstates its current wiring: it is defense-in-depth wired at download, with its other rules independently enforced inline, by the version model, and by the contract readiness engine. That is architecture hygiene / redundancy, not a document-integrity defect — and the auditor themselves concede they can produce no failing scenario ("the practical blast radius is currently limited").

The structural observation is accurate (enforceDocumentGuard has one production call site, download, at documents.ts:244; pierre_rt_document_versions has no approved_content_hash column), but there is NO reachable input that produces the claimed bad outcome, and two load-bearing sub-claims are false.

(1) UNREACHABLE — the disciplinary/payroll scenario cannot be constructed. No API route imports v1/documents.ts (the src/app/api/pierre/documents/** routes are preview/render/validate on a different module). The only production importers are contracts.ts, signatures.ts (createVersion on an already-existing contract document), and runtime-compensation-execution.ts (archiveDocument). The single production createDocument call is contracts.ts:263 passing `policy.document_type`, and contract-policies.ts:44 hardcodes `document_type: "employment_contract"` in the policy() factory — none of the 11 CONTRACT_POLICIES overrides it, and `amendment_document_type` is declared but never read anywhere in the repo. So a 'disciplinary_document' or 'payroll_variable_document' can never be created, approved, or finalized through any entry point. The guard's payroll/disciplinary branches are unreachable, not merely unwired. The claim concedes this itself by resting its impact on "any current or future caller" — future-caller risk is hardening, not a defect.

(2) The rules are ENFORCED on the one reachable path. approveVersion/finalizeVersion have exactly one production caller: driveDocumentVersionToFinal (contracts.ts:371) <- finalizeContract (contracts.ts:360). finalizeContract calls resolveReadiness(...,'finalize',...) and throws Errors.conflict BEFORE the transaction, blocking on template_not_published (contract-readiness.ts:84), missing_required_fields (:111), document_hash_drift (:118/124 — the guard's approval_invalidated_by_change), artifact_not_clean (:125) and insufficient_approvals (:122). These are the exact rules the claim says are "never enforced".

(3) The claim "the guard's hash-comparison inputs have no source of truth anywhere in the product" is FALSE. contracts.ts:326-328 records the approval bound to canonical_hash + template_fingerprint in pierre_rt_contract_approvals, and contracts.ts:160-161 only counts approvals whose content_hash still matches the current canonical_hash — so a post-approval content change drops approvals_valid to 0 and blocks finalize. Separately, pierre_rt_signature_requests.approved_content_hash exists (migration line 225) and signatures.ts:510 fails closed without it. The content-to-approval binding lives on the contract/signature tables rather than on document_versions.

Verdict: real architectural observation (the guard's docstring overstates its wiring), zero reachable failure. Refuted as unreachable / gated upstream.

refutedSummary.title: Cockpit permission object fails OPEN: absent/empty permission keys yield all-true DEFAULT_PERMISSIONS, showing Approve/Cancel affordances to users who cannot use them
why: The quoted fail-open branch in permissionsFromKeys (permissions.ts:28) is never reached in production. A whole-src search shows the only non-test references to permissionsFromKeys are its own definition (line 27) and a doc comment (line 17); every callsite that actually invokes it lives under __tests__/. All real render paths hardcode DEFAULT_PERMISSIONS directly (useOperationalCockpit.ts:101; useCloneChat.ts:98/199/200/208) and never derive permissions from server keys, so the "absent/empty keys yield all-true DEFAULT_PERMISSIONS" mechanism the claim describes does not execute at runtime. Separately, the claim itself concedes this is NOT an authorization bypass: the server enforces requirePermission and returns 403 on every mutation (approve/cancel/reschedule all hit the V1 API), and the all-true UI default is documented, intentional design (permissions.ts:14-17; useOperationalCockpit.ts:101 comment "serveur = autorite finale a chaque mutation"). The UI already contains working denied-affordance rendering (v1.ts:200-212, map.ts:116-128 emit allowed:false with a role reason) that engages whenever a restricted CockpitPermissions object is threaded; production just never threads one, by design, rather than via a fail-open regression at the quoted line. Thus the specific defect is unreachable and mischaracterized, and the residual UX concern is an intentional, server-authoritative design choice.

The claim is scoped to a specific defect: `permissionsFromKeys` (permissions.ts:27-28) fails OPEN, returning all-true DEFAULT_PERMISSIONS for null/empty keys, and this "silently degrades" the cockpit into showing Approve/Cancel/Reschedule affordances. The fail-open branch is real, BUT the claimed impact does not follow, on three grounds:

1) DEAD RELATIVE TO RENDERING. `permissionsFromKeys` has ZERO production callers. A repo-wide grep excluding __tests__ returns only its own definition and a doc comment; the only invocations are in test files (permissions.test.ts, map.test.ts, v1.test.ts, engine.test.ts, action-policy.test.ts, openai-layer.test.ts). The two real cockpit consumers — src/app/assistant/useCloneChat.ts (lines 98, 199-200, 208) and src/app/agents/pierre/use/hooks/useOperationalCockpit.ts (line 101: `const permissions: CockpitPermissions = DEFAULT_PERMISSIONS;`) — hardcode DEFAULT_PERMISSIONS unconditionally and never thread server keys through permissionsFromKeys. So the "key-plumbing regression that silently degrades permissionsFromKeys into all-true" cannot occur: there is no key plumbing to regress, and fixing line 27 to fail-closed would change nothing in the shipped UI. The all-affordances behavior comes from the deliberate, documented hardcoded DEFAULT_PERMISSIONS in the hooks, not from the line-27 fail-open the claim names.

2) NOT AN AUTH BYPASS (conceded). The claim itself concedes server authority holds (requirePermission → 403). roles.ts confirms every mutation path is guarded by requirePermission(ctx, ...). No duplicate external effect, false success, tenant leak, or unsafe autonomous decision results.

3) CONSEQUENCE MISCHARACTERIZED. The claim says the failure "surfaces as an opaque error rather than a hidden/disabled control." The design contradicts this: validationActions (map.ts:116-128) emits actions carrying `allowed:false` plus a human reason ("Votre rôle ne permet pas de décider des validations.") when canDecideValidations is false — i.e., the intended UX is a disabled/annotated control, not an opaque error.

Net: the fail-open at line 27 has no shipped-behavior consequence (no rendering path reaches it), the security consequence is nil (server authority, conceded), and the "misleading state" is a separate, deliberate, documented design choice rather than the named defect. The impact attributed to permissions.ts:27 is overstated/misattributed. Refuted.

The only remaining `sent` communication case is `low_risk_notification`, whose executor (executors.ts:56-64) really inserts a pierre_rt_notifications row and returns delivered:"in_app" — a genuine completed delivery, so "Envoyé" is truthful there, not a fabricated success. The claim's core grievance is already fixed in-code.

The claim quotes pre-fix code that no longer exists. The claimed line 278 (`else if (DONE_TASK.has(status)) artStatus = isComm && !isDoc ? "sent" : "validated";`) has been superseded by a P16D guard. Reproduction of the primary/titled scenario is now blocked, and a dedicated test enforces it.

Traced call chain for the claimed input "Relancer Marie sur son justificatif avant vendredi":
1. analysis.ts:54 OPERATIONAL_RULES `/\b(relance|relancer)/i` → action `reminder`, task type `reminder` (analysis.ts:207 `type: r.action`).
2. autonomy.ts:69-70: `reminder` ∈ AUTO_EXECUTE_ACTIONS, risk low, external_side_effect false → AUTO_EXECUTE → task reaches `succeeded`.
3. executors.ts:66-72: `reminder` returns `{kind:"reminder", scheduled_for}`, external_side_effect:false — nothing sent (accurate premise).
4. v1.ts deriveV1Artifacts: type "reminder" matches COMM_RE, not DOC_RE. But at v1.ts:290 the current branch is `isComm && !isDoc ? (SCHEDULE_ONLY_TASK.has(type) ? "scheduled" : "sent") : "validated"`, and SCHEDULE_ONLY_TASK (v1.ts:74) = {"reminder","deadline_reminder"}. So artStatus = "scheduled", NOT "sent".
5. status.ts:194: artifactStatusView("scheduled") = { label:"Planifié", tone:"neutral" }. The chip is "Planifié" / neutral — NOT "Envoyé", NOT success.

So `reminder` and `deadline_reminder` (the two schedule-only executors the claim names) both render "Planifié"/neutral. The regression test p16d-truthful-status.test.ts:28-38 asserts exactly this ("scheduled"/"Planifié", tone !== "success"), and email_send stays "blocked"→"À relire" (never "Envoyé").

The only residual is `low_risk_notification` (not in SCHEDULE_ONLY_TASK) → still "sent"/"Envoyé". But this is NOT the claimed false success: the internalNotification executor (executors.ts:56-64) actually INSERTS a real pierre_rt_notifications row and returns `delivered:"in_app"`, so a delivery genuinely occurs — contradicting the claim's core assertions ("qui n'a JAMAIS été envoyée", "aucune ligne d'outbox", "la relance n'est même pas rédigée"). The severity-high scenario (nothing sent, not even drafted) applied only to `reminder`, which is now guarded. Verdict: refuted — quoted line is stale and the primary reachable path no longer produces the bad outcome.
